title: A Big Year for M&A, but Only 2% of Companies Are Actually Using AI
dek: Gene Sykes, Goldman Sachs' co-head of M&A, says this is the biggest M&A year in history, driven by AI infrastructure — but only 2% of companies are seeing AI lift EPS in their reported results.
why: The first half is about selling sponsorships for the Los Angeles Olympics and transportation details; the second half is where M&A, AI adoption rates and media asset pricing come in. Medium information density.
who: Investors watching AI capex and the M&A cycle, founders working on enterprise AI deployment, and anyone who wants to understand the business structure of a major sporting event.
skip: The opening chit-chat about Huntington Beach and California livability, and the host's closing subscription and community plug.

points.h: The Olympics is an order of magnitude bigger than the World Cup
points.body: Gene Sykes offers the comparison: the World Cup was held across Mexico, the United States and Canada, with 104 matches, 16 stadiums and roughly 600 athletes. The Los Angeles Olympics and Paralympics together will have 17,000 athletes, about 900 medal events, and 15 million tickets sold across the two — the World Cup sold only 6.5 million. His claim is that the Olympics covers roughly 90% of the sports world you can imagine. That scale difference puts the organizational complexity on an entirely different level.

points.h: Los Angeles doesn't have to build a single venue
points.body: On the so-called ‘first privately funded Olympics’, Sykes' explanation is this: no government money is going into running the Games, and the federal government only plays a role in security and related logistics, because 206 countries will be sending teams. It can be done this way because Southern California already has the best sports infrastructure in the world — the venues and arenas are all there, nothing new needs to be built. The athletes' village doesn't need to be built either; everyone stays in UCLA dorms — UCLA normally houses more students than the athletes needed during the Olympics. This is the key to why these Games are easier to plan and execute.

points.h: Media rights were sold a decade in advance
points.body: Part of the Olympics' money is ‘pre-baked’: the International Olympic Committee sells the media rights for all the Games many years ahead of time, NBC is the U.S. rights holder, and the contract already runs to 2036 — by which point nobody even knows where the Olympics will be held. The U.S. rights fee is $1.5 billion or more per Games. The IOC also sells sponsorships to companies like Coca-Cola, Visa and Samsung. Then the domestic organizing committee sells another round, and for Los Angeles that went to Starbucks, Uber and Google. Sykes says corporate interest is enormous, because everyone believes this will be the biggest event in world history.

points.h: This is the biggest M&A year in history
points.body: Sykes says this is the biggest M&A year in world history, and by a wide margin. The previous peak was 2021, and that was inflated by COVID. Over the past few years, 40% of the M&A market was sales of private-equity-owned companies; this year that share has fallen to 30%, because more substantive demand has appeared — around AI's impact on the economy, every industry is going through the same thing, natural resources and power generation alike, because they are building AI infrastructure. There has been a huge boom in semiconductor technology and semiconductor M&A, because everyone wants to own proprietary semiconductor technology.

points.h: 80% of startups end by being acquired
points.body: Sykes' judgment is this: every startup, even an AI company, has to think clearly about what its endgame is, and 80% of startups end by selling themselves to someone else. That is both the calculation in the founder's head and the source of economic return for the VCs behind them — you have to think clearly about how what you build helps another piece of the puzzle. The remaining 20% can become durably independent companies, either because they have something completely differentiated or because they simply can't find a buyer. He cites SpaceX as an example: in a market that already had plenty of incumbents, it did something different, and those incumbents were constrained by the regulatory environment, so SpaceX chose to challenge it.

points.h: Anthropic and OpenAI are too big for anyone to buy
points.body: Sykes says Anthropic and OpenAI will obviously become independent companies, because they are almost too big for anyone to buy. That's the other side: if a company gets too big, it means it has succeeded very well, but you have to have enough confidence that they own a durable platform. Tracey follows up: will we one day read in the risk factors of an S-1, ‘we believe there is a non-trivial probability that our technology will wipe out all of humanity’? Sykes says lawyers would probably say you need to protect yourself and make sure disclosure is complete, so that kind of big, crazy, scary thing will definitely show up in S-1 language.

points.h: This infrastructure build is funded from free cash flow
points.body: On the analogy between AI infrastructure and the TMT bubble, Sykes says there's no way to know how big the market will be or whether it will be overbuilt relative to real demand five or six years out — the answer is ‘we just don't know’. But he points to one key difference: in 2000 and 2001, during the first TMT internet buildout, the money came mainly from VCs; this buildout is funded by the world's most successful large technology platforms, which until this year had hundreds of billions of dollars in free cash flow. That is an astonishing reversal.

points.h: Only 2% are actually seeing AI lift EPS
points.body: Joe offers a theory: enterprise AI adoption is basically zero. Sykes says they just ran the analysis, and it's 2% — meaning the companies that say in their reported results that their use of AI has had a positive impact on EPS, currently only 2%. He distinguishes several levels: maybe 20% to 30% of companies have implemented a strategy of using AI across their businesses; but employees each having a ChatGPT or Claude subscription and using it as ‘glorified search’ doesn't count as meaningful adoption. He uses Goldman itself as an example: a huge number of prompts are being used to do things with AI, and the youngest employees are ‘AI natives’, doing things that were unimaginable a year ago.

points.h: AI won't replace the relationship side of M&A
points.body: Sykes says M&A is a business of trusted relationships and good advice, and clients are looking for people who understand the world and can synthesize a lot of independent variables. Synthesizing independent variables is a talent, and people who are good at it get stronger with AI: they reach conclusions faster, and they're more imaginative — after getting the first data point they don't take it at face value, they ask the reverse question. His wording is careful: it's not that people get smarter, it's that if they can get more and better information, they can have more confidence and better judgment. He thinks this will reshape how everyone in the industry gives advice, and how clients understand what to expect.

points.h: AI will make old film libraries more valuable
points.body: On whether content libraries and rights libraries become more or less valuable, Sykes says they have been getting more valuable for the past decade, partly because some people want to securitize the cash flows. He personally believes familiarity, things already validated by time and widely appreciated, are very valuable, so they will keep getting more valuable. And AI is very likely to make existing content libraries more valuable, because it will find more uses for existing content. He imagines AI creating an environment where people are reached in ‘pulses’ by different types of media content in ways they never imagined, and where AI is smart enough to make that reaching actually appealing to people, rather than bombarding them into annoyance.
